headline: Hau is written with 這, a kokkun not derived from the Chinese kanbun tradition.
Sou is from Old Japanese 沿ふ (sopu), used in the Man'yōshū.
Byōdō was originally a Buddhist term, hence the goon reading, and is first cited to a text from 927.
In kōsaten, 差 is a daiyōji replacing 叉.
Un is an onomatopoeia of the grunting noise made when straining oneself in effort.
Itsumademo is いつ (itsu, “when”) plus まで (made, “until, up to”) plus も (mo, “even, also”): literally “until even any time”.
Shōjō is from Middle Chinese 癥狀, “abdominal tumor, disease + form, appearance”.
Nayamu appears in the Man'yōshū of 759 and may derive from 萎える (naeru, “to weaken; to wither”).
Ana is first attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE, from Proto-Japonic *ana.
Sumimasen is the negative of 済む (sumu, “to finish; to be settled”): literally “(the trouble) is not settled”.
Ogenki de is お (o, honorific marker) plus 元気 (genki, “healthy”) plus で (de, particle for location).
Gojūon is 五十 (gojū, “fifty”) plus 音 (-on, “sound”).
Sukuu is cognate with 掬う.
Shoku, “employment”, is from Middle Chinese 職 (MC tsyik).
Sokuryoku is 速 (soku, “fast”) plus 力 (-ryoku, “power”).
Soto appears from roughly the Muromachi period, likely 背 (so, “back, behind”) plus 外 (to, “outside”) or 所 (to, “place”).
Hara, “field”, is compared with Middle Korean ᄇᆞᆯ (pól), whence modern 벌 (beol).
Iyoiyo is a reduplication of the archaic adverb いよ (iyo, “more and more, increasingly”).
Mōsu, the humble “to say”, was mawosu in Old Japanese.
Kirau is first attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE; the Daijiten lists it as cognate with 切る (kiru, “to cut”), but Samuel Martin thinks that unlikely.
Terasu is originally the causative of 照る (teru, “to shine”): “to make shine”.
Nodo, “throat”, may come from nomito: 飲み (nomi, “to drink”) plus 門 (to, “gate, door”).
Dō shite mo is どうして plus も.
Bu, the negative prefix, is from Middle Chinese 不 (MC pjuw).
Hada went from pada through ɸada to hada, from Proto-Japonic *panta.
Gomu is borrowed from Dutch gom, “gum”.
Yoi is the modern form of the Old Japanese adjective よし (yoshi).
Mitsu, “thick, close”, is from Middle Chinese 密 (MC mit), first cited to a text from 1092.
Kitto is a gemination of きと (kito).
Tokoro is likely cognate with 床 (toko, “raised area; bed”), and first attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.
